title: Rooms of the keep
description: Remember what is in every room of the keep, look a room up by its name, and cope with a room that is not there.

tasks.title: Look things up by name
tasks.body: A dictionary pairs each key with a value: rooms = {"hall": "lamp", "cellar": "rope"}. rooms["hall"] gives "lamp". Keys must match exactly, so "Hall" is a different key.
tasks.detail: rooms["tower"] = "key" adds a pair, or replaces the value if that key is already there. rooms["attic"], for a key that is not there, stops with a KeyError; rooms.get("attic", "nothing") gives "nothing" instead. for room, item in rooms.items(): visits each pair, in the order the keys were first added.

tasks.code:
# What is in each room?
rooms = {"hall": "lamp", "cellar": "rope"}
rooms["tower"] = "key"
rooms["hall"] = "map"
print(rooms["cellar"])
print(rooms.get("attic", "nothing"))
for room, item in rooms.items():
    print(room, item)
tasks.output:
rope
nothing
hall map
cellar rope
tower key
tasks.note: hall already had a value, so it changed to map without moving. get() gives its second value for a key that is missing. items() goes through the pairs in the order the keys were first added.

tasks.question: What would print(rooms["attic"]) do here?
tasks.why: Square brackets need the key to be there. get() is the gentle way to ask about a key that may be missing.

tasks.prompt: Predict, then run: print len(rooms), add a fourth room, and print it again. Then look up "Hall", with a capital, using get(), and see what comes back.

Each room of the keep holds one thing. Ask how many rooms there are, then for each room ask for its name and then what it holds. A room named twice is one room, holding the thing given last. Then ask for a room to search. Print three lines: what the searched room holds, or empty if there is no such room; how many rooms there are; and the whole dictionary, with print(). Print just those three lines.
tasks.starter: # Read each room and what it holds, then the room to search
hints: Make an empty dictionary, {}, before the loop. Each time round, read a name and a thing, and pair them, with the name as the key.
Assigning to a key that is already there replaces its value, which is just what a room named twice needs. get() with a second value answers for a room that is not there.
With other names: prices = {} before the loop, then prices[fruit] = cost inside it. prices.get(fruit, 0) gives 0 for a fruit with no price.

error_hints.text: That room is not a key in the dictionary. get() with a second value answers without stopping the program.
range() needs a whole number: use int(...) on the number of rooms.
Your program asked for more replies than it gets. Each room has two replies, its name and then its thing, and the room to search comes after the loop.
Make the dictionary before the loop uses it, and spell its name the same way every time.
With hall, cellar and tower, searching cellar gives rope. Check which reply is the key and which is the value: the name is the key.
A room that is not there gives the word empty, not None and not an error.
A room named twice keeps the thing given last. Assigning to the same key again replaces its value.
Check a keep with no rooms: the count is 0 and print() shows an empty dictionary as {}.
Check names that differ only in capital letters: keys must match exactly, so they are different rooms.

similar_example.note: Names and ages instead of rooms and things: a new key adds a pair, an old key gets a new value, and get() answers for a missing one.

other_ways.note: in works on a dictionary too: it checks the keys. Once you know the key is there, square brackets are safe.

other_ways.code:
count = int(input("Rooms? "))
rooms = {}
while count > 0:
    name = input("Room? ")
    thing = input("Holds? ")
    rooms.update({name: thing})
    count -= 1
print(rooms.get(input("Search? "), "empty"))
print(len(rooms))
print(rooms)
other_ways.note: update() adds every pair of another dictionary, replacing values for keys already there. The search reply can go straight into get().
